claim: ATAC-seq was performed on E15.5 mouse proximal and distal femoral growth zones.
source: In order to identify open chromatin regions involved in long bone development, we performed ATAC-seq (Buenrostro et al., 2015, 2013) on E15.5 (Theiler Stage 23) mouse proximal and distal femoral growth zones, regions comprised predominately of the growth plate proper, the overlying perichondrium, and the cartilaginous super-structures that dictate adult bony morphology (Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the experimental procedure performed on specific mouse tissues at a defined developmental stage.

claim: E15.5 of mouse embryogenesis corresponds to approximately E48-51 (Carnegie Stage 19) of human development.
source: This stage of mouse embryogenesis corresponds to approximately E48-51 (Carnegie Stage 19) of human development and reflects a developmental window when the growth plate proper possesses all chondrocyte zones (resting, proliferative, pre-hypertrophic, hypertrophic zone) and is undergoing rapid cell proliferation and differentiation during endochondral ossification.
evidence: The manuscript provides a direct comparison between mouse and human developmental stages based on established knowledge.

claim: The growth plate at E15.5 possesses all chondrocyte zones (resting, proliferative, pre-hypertrophic, hypertrophic zone).
source: This stage of mouse embryogenesis corresponds to approximately E48-51 (Carnegie Stage 19) of human development and reflects a developmental window when the growth plate proper possesses all chondrocyte zones (resting, proliferative, pre-hypertrophic, hypertrophic zone) and is undergoing rapid cell proliferation and differentiation during endochondral ossification.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the composition of the growth plate at the studied developmental stage.

claim: ATAC-seq yielded 28,257 proximal femur peaks and 27,958 distal femur peaks.
source: This approach yielded 28,257 proximal femur peaks and 27,958 distal femur peaks, with 23,764 shared peaks, 4493 peaks specific to the proximal femur, and 4194 specific to the distal femur (Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific quantitative results from the ATAC-seq experiment, also shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 23,764 ATAC-seq peaks are shared between proximal and distal femur samples.
source: This approach yielded 28,257 proximal femur peaks and 27,958 distal femur peaks, with 23,764 shared peaks, 4493 peaks specific to the proximal femur, and 4194 specific to the distal femur (Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative overlap data between the two sample types.

claim: Proximal femur ATAC-seq peaks span approximately 0.79% of the genome.
source: The proximal and distal peaks span approximately 0.79% and 0.76% of the genome, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports the genomic coverage of the identified peaks.

claim: Distal femur ATAC-seq peaks span approximately 0.76% of the genome.
source: The proximal and distal peaks span approximately 0.79% and 0.76% of the genome, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports the genomic coverage of the identified peaks.

claim: ATAC-seq peaks show characteristic enrichment near gene transcriptional start sites and distal intronic and intergenic non-coding sequences.
source: We also assessed the genomic distribution of proximal and distal femur ATAC-seq peaks and found a characteristic enrichment near gene transcriptional start sites and more distal intronic and intergenic non-coding sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the genomic distribution pattern of the peaks, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Liftover of mouse femur open chromatin regions to the human genome resulted in 24,805 proximal femur peaks and 24,788 distal femur peaks.
source: Our liftover resulted in 24,805 proximal femur peaks and 24,788 distal femur peaks, representing approximately 87.7% and 88.6% of sites identified in mouse, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of the liftover procedure from mouse to human genome.

claim: 87.7% of proximal femur peaks and 88.6% of distal femur peaks were successfully lifted over to the human genome.
source: Our liftover resulted in 24,805 proximal femur peaks and 24,788 distal femur peaks, representing approximately 87.7% and 88.6% of sites identified in mouse, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript provides the percentage of peaks that could be mapped to the human genome.

claim: Sites capable of liftover to human likely reflect relatively conserved genes involved in vertebrate musculoskeletal development.
source: These sites that were capable of liftover to human likely reflect relatively conserved genes involved in vertebrate musculoskeletal development (Shubin et al., 1997; Petit et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the liftover results in the context of evolutionary conservation, supported by citations.

claim: The union of proximal and distal lifted-over peaks contained 25,829 peaks.
source: The union of the two sets contained 25,829 peaks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the total number of unique peaks after combining proximal and distal datasets.

claim: ATAC-seq peaks are enriched near genes with phenotype terms related to skeletal development, chondrogenesis, and long bone skeletal phenotypes.
source: They also yielded phenotype terms related to general skeletal development, chondrogenesis, and long bone skeletal phenotypes, such as 'Metaphyseal widening', 'Abnormality of the femoral epiphyses', and 'Abnormality of the femoral head' (Figure 1c).
evidence: The manuscript reports GREAT analysis results showing enrichment for skeletal-related phenotypes, shown in Figure 1c.

claim: ATAC-seq peaks are enriched for GO Biological Processes such as 'Cartilage condensation', 'Positive regulation of chondrocyte differentiation', and 'Chondrocyte proliferation'.
source: For example, GREAT analyses uncovered enrichment for several relevant GO Biological Processes such as 'Cartilage condensation', 'Positive regulation of chondrocyte differentiation', and 'Chondrocyte proliferation' (Supplementary file 2–4).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific GO terms enriched near ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: 86.4% of Class I Sox9 elements overlap with femur ATAC-seq peaks.
source: For example, 86.4% of Class I Sox9 elements (i.e. elements clustering near transcriptional start sites of highly expressed non-chondrocyte-specific genes), 44.6% of Class II Sox9 elements (i.e. elements directing chondrocyte-related gene activity through direct Sox9 dimer binding), and 93.8% of Sox9 super-enhancer regions (i.e. enhancer complexes involved in chondrocyte cell identity) overlap with our femur ATAC-seq peaks (p<0.001 for all three sets, Materials and methods, Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative overlap between Sox9 ChIP-seq data and ATAC-seq peaks with statistical significance.

claim: 44.6% of Class II Sox9 elements overlap with femur ATAC-seq peaks.
source: For example, 86.4% of Class I Sox9 elements (i.e. elements clustering near transcriptional start sites of highly expressed non-chondrocyte-specific genes), 44.6% of Class II Sox9 elements (i.e. elements directing chondrocyte-related gene activity through direct Sox9 dimer binding), and 93.8% of Sox9 super-enhancer regions (i.e. enhancer complexes involved in chondrocyte cell identity) overlap with our femur ATAC-seq peaks (p<0.001 for all three sets, Materials and methods, Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative overlap between Sox9 ChIP-seq data and ATAC-seq peaks with statistical significance.

claim: 93.8% of Sox9 super-enhancer regions overlap with femur ATAC-seq peaks.
source: For example, 86.4% of Class I Sox9 elements (i.e. elements clustering near transcriptional start sites of highly expressed non-chondrocyte-specific genes), 44.6% of Class II Sox9 elements (i.e. elements directing chondrocyte-related gene activity through direct Sox9 dimer binding), and 93.8% of Sox9 super-enhancer regions (i.e. enhancer complexes involved in chondrocyte cell identity) overlap with our femur ATAC-seq peaks (p<0.001 for all three sets, Materials and methods, Figure 2a).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative overlap between Sox9 ChIP-seq data and ATAC-seq peaks with statistical significance.

claim: 85.1% of RNA Pol II transcriptionally active promoters overlap with femur ATAC-seq peaks.
source: We found that 85.1% of RNA Pol II transcriptionally active promoters, 56.9% of H3K4me2 active promoter sites, 86.7% of H3K4me3 active promoter sites, 87.4% of H3K27ac active enhancer sites, and 59.4% of p300 histone acetyltransferase active enhancer sites overlapped with femur ATAC-seq peaks.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative overlap between various histone modifications and ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: 56.9% of H3K4me2 active promoter sites overlap with femur ATAC-seq peaks.
source: We found that 85.1% of RNA Pol II transcriptionally active promoters, 56.9% of H3K4me2 active promoter sites, 86.7% of H3K4me3 active promoter sites, 87.4% of H3K27ac active enhancer sites, and 59.4% of p300 histone acetyltransferase active enhancer sites overlapped with femur ATAC-seq peaks.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative overlap between various histone modifications and ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: 86.7% of H3K4me3 active promoter sites overlap with femur ATAC-seq peaks.
source: We found that 85.1% of RNA Pol II transcriptionally active promoters, 56.9% of H3K4me2 active promoter sites, 86.7% of H3K4me3 active promoter sites, 87.4% of H3K27ac active enhancer sites, and 59.4% of p300 histone acetyltransferase active enhancer sites overlapped with femur ATAC-seq peaks.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative overlap between various histone modifications and ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: 87.4% of H3K27ac active enhancer sites overlap with femur ATAC-seq peaks.
source: We found that 85.1% of RNA Pol II transcriptionally active promoters, 56.9% of H3K4me2 active promoter sites, 86.7% of H3K4me3 active promoter sites, 87.4% of H3K27ac active enhancer sites, and 59.4% of p300 histone acetyltransferase active enhancer sites overlapped with femur ATAC-seq peaks.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative overlap between various histone modifications and ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: 59.4% of p300 histone acetyltransferase active enhancer sites overlap with femur ATAC-seq peaks.
source: We found that 85.1% of RNA Pol II transcriptionally active promoters, 56.9% of H3K4me2 active promoter sites, 86.7% of H3K4me3 active promoter sites, 87.4% of H3K27ac active enhancer sites, and 59.4% of p300 histone acetyltransferase active enhancer sites overlapped with femur ATAC-seq peaks.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative overlap between various histone modifications and ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: Only 33.7% of H3K27me3-repressed enhancer sites overlap with femur ATAC-seq signals.
source: Conversely, our ATAC-seq datasets displayed relatively lower overlap with markers of gene repression; that is, only 33.7% of H3K27me3-repressed enhancer sites overlap with femur ATAC-seq signals (Figure 2b).
evidence: The manuscript reports lower overlap with repressive histone marks compared to active marks.

claim: The enrichments of all histone modification sets with ATAC-seq peaks were significant at p<0.001.
source: Based on permutation analyses, the enrichments of all these histone modification sets were significant at p<0.001.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical significance of the overlap analyses.

claim: 45.2% of E47 human limb bud H3K27ac peaks overlap with ATAC-seq peaks.
source: We found that 45.2% of these E47 human limb bud H3K27ac peaks overlapped with ATAC-seq peaks, indicating that many of our mouse femur ATAC-seq peaks reflect active human limb enhancers involved in chondrogenesis (p<0.001, Figure 2c).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative overlap with human limb bud data with statistical significance.

claim: 13.3% of human adult BMDC H3K27ac peaks overlap with mouse distal femur ATAC-seq dataset.
source: Second, we used an H3K27ac ChIP-seq dataset generated on human adult cultured bone marrow mesenchymal stem-cell-derived chondrocytes (BMDCs) (Herlofsen et al., 2013; Kundaje et al., 2015) and found that 13.3% of human adult BMDC H3K27ac peaks overlapped our mouse distal femur dataset (p<0.001) (Figure 2c), which indicates that our femur ATAC-seq dataset also captures cell-intrinsic properties of chondrogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative overlap with human BMDC data with statistical significance.

claim: ATAC-seq data identified 14 of 26 previously-discovered active regulatory elements near key cartilage genes.
source: Our ATAC-seq data were also able to identify 14 of 26 previously-discovered active regulatory elements residing near key cartilage genes detected at different time-points and using different assays (e.g. see Figure 2d, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports the ability to recapitulate previously known regulatory elements.

claim: 317 height GWAS loci (approximately 46%) contain at least one variant that overlaps with an ATAC-seq peak.
source: Across the 688 height loci, we found that 317 loci (or ~46%) contained at least one variant that overlapped with an ATAC-seq peak.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number and percentage of height GWAS loci overlapping ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: Height GWAS variants show strong enrichment at ATAC-seq peaks (p=0.0059) using GoShifter analysis.
source: We found strong enrichments for the ATAC-seq peak set and height GWAS data (p=0.0059) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical enrichment using GoShifter permutation analysis.

claim: Only mouse rib chondrocyte H3K4me2 peaks reached statistical significance (p=0.0237) in GoShifter analysis with height GWAS data.
source: Only the mouse rib chondrocyte H3K4me2 peaks reached statistical significance (p=0.0237), and was far less significant than our ATAC-seq data.
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative GoShifter results for different epigenetic datasets.

claim: No enrichment was observed for height GWAS variants at DNaseI hypersensitivity sites from mouse brain, liver, and lung.
source: Also, as no enrichment was observed for other mouse tissues from ENCODE, this suggests that the observed enrichment is unlikely due to artifacts stemming from our use of mouse tissues (e.g. from conserved regions being lifted over).
evidence: The manuscript reports lack of enrichment in non-skeletal tissues as a control.

claim: Height GWAS loci are enriched near 427 differentially expressed growth plate genes when compared to matched random GWAS loci (p<0.001, z-score: 8.54).
source: We expanded on those results using the most recent height GWAS from Wood et al. (2014) and indeed found that height GWAS loci are enriched near 427 differentially expressed growth plate genes (within 100 kb) when compared to the 1000 matched random GWAS loci (p<0.001, z-score: 8.54, Figure 5a).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical enrichment of height GWAS loci near differentially expressed growth plate genes.

claim: 46 of 688 height GWAS loci (approximately 6.7%) contain at least one GWAS variant that overlaps with an ATAC-seq peak and resides near a differentially expressed gene.
source: We again used the 688 GWAS loci from Wood et al. (2014) and their proxy SNPs (r2 >0.5) and found that 46/688 loci (or ~6.7%) contained at least one GWAS variant that overlapped with an ATAC-seq peak and resided near a differentially expressed gene (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number and percentage of loci meeting multiple criteria.

claim: The overlap of height GWAS variants with ATAC-seq peaks near differentially expressed genes is highly significant (p<0.001, z-score: 6.36).
source: Using the same 1000 sets of matched random loci as described above, we found that these overlaps were highly significant (p<0.001, z-score: 6.36, Figure 5b).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical significance of the combined enrichment.

claim: eQTL variants for 157 differentially expressed growth plate genes are significantly enriched at ATAC-seq peaks (p=0.0004).
source: Using the GoShifter permutation analysis as described above, we demonstrated that the corresponding eQTL variants for these 157 genes are significantly enriched at ATAC-seq peaks (p=0.0004)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical enrichment of eQTL variants at ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: 59 variants distributed across 26 loci are in the PICS 95% credible set, overlap an ATAC-seq peak, and are near a differentially expressed growth plate gene.
source: In total, 59 variants distributed across 26 loci met these criteria.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of variants meeting stringent filtering criteria.

claim: rs9920291 is predicted to alter HOXD13 binding based on universal protein binding microarray technology.
source: Of the four variants, rs9920291 is predicted to alter HOXD13 binding, as suggested by data generated using universal protein binding microarray technology that demonstrates that the eight base-pair sequence matching the immediate rs9920291 locus disrupts in vitro binding by HOXD13 (Figure 6a, Supplementary file 7), a homeodomain transcription factor that is expressed in the growth plate (Kuss et al., 2014; Reno et al., 2016) and has known activating and repressive roles in skeletal development (Johnson and Tabin, 1997).
evidence: The manuscript reports computational prediction of transcription factor binding disruption supported by experimental data.

claim: The open chromatin region surrounding rs9920291 acts as a repressor of expression in T/C-28a2 human chondrocytes (p=7.83×10−6 for reference allele and p=3.6×10−4 for alternate allele).
source: First, using a luciferase reporter assay in T/C-28a2 human chondrocytes, we found that the open chromatin region surrounding rs9920291 acts as a repressor of expression (p=7.83×10−6 and 3.6 × 10−4 for variants carrying the reference and alternate alleles respectively) (Figure 6b).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from luciferase assays with statistical significance.

claim: The alternate T allele of rs9920291 makes the regulatory element act as a weaker repressor (p=0.0014).
source: In addition, the alternate T allele, (i.e. the height-increasing allele of rs9920291) makes the regulatory element act as a weaker repressor (p=0.0014).
evidence: The manuscript reports differential regulatory activity between alleles with statistical significance.

claim: rs9920291 acts as an eQTL for CHSY1 in transformed fibroblasts (p=1.0×10-7) with the T allele correlating with increased CHSY1 expression levels.
source: This is consistent with data from GTEx (Lonsdale J, GTEx Consortium, 2013), where rs9920291 acts as an eQTL for CHSY1 in transformed fibroblasts (p=1.0×10-7; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), with the T allele correlating with increased CHSY1 expression levels.
evidence: The manuscript reports eQTL data from GTEx with statistical significance.

claim: rs9920291 displays allelic skew in expression in HEK-293FT cells (p<0.001 for both assayed variants).
source: Assaying a heterozygous exonic coding SNP (rs28364839) and a 3'UTR SNP (rs11433), we demonstrate that rs9920291 displays allelic skew in expression (p<0.001 for both assayed variants; Figure 6d).
evidence: The manuscript reports allelic expression imbalance with statistical significance.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated deletion of a 135 bp region surrounding rs9920291 leads to significant upregulation of CHSY1 expression (p=7.83×10−6).
source: Either deletion led to a significant upregulation of CHSY1 expression in vitro in T/C-28a2 cells (p=7.83×10−6 for the 135 bp deletion and p=3.64×10−4 for the 17 bp deletion; Figure 6d), confirming the regulatory element's repressor activity.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from CRISPR deletion with statistical significance.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated deletion of a 17 bp region immediately surrounding rs9920291 leads to significant upregulation of CHSY1 expression (p=3.64×10−4).
source: Either deletion led to a significant upregulation of CHSY1 expression in vitro in T/C-28a2 cells (p=7.83×10−6 for the 135 bp deletion and p=3.64×10−4 for the 17 bp deletion; Figure 6d), confirming the regulatory element's repressor activity.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from CRISPR deletion with statistical significance.

claim: Overexpression of HOXD13 in T/C-28a2 cells significantly upregulates CHSY1 expression (p=1.63×10−5).
source: Consistent with our computational predictions that rs9920291 perturbs HOXD13 binding, we found that overexpression of HOXD13 in T/C-28a2 cells significantly upregulated CHSY1 expression (p=1.63×10−5; Figure 6e,Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from overexpression experiments with statistical significance.

claim: De novo motif analysis identified enriched transcription-factor-binding motifs including Atf3, Msx2, Pbx1, and Ctcf in ATAC-seq peaks.
source: We identified a number of highly enriched motifs relevant to chondrogenesis and other skeletal developmental processes, including Atf3 (James et al., 2006), Msx2 (Amano et al., 2008), Pbx1 (Selleri et al., 2001), and Ctcf (Jerković et al., 2017) (Figure 7a, Supplementary file 8, sheet 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports motif enrichment results with citations supporting their relevance.

claim: Height GWAS variants within ATAC-seq peaks show enrichment for variants predicted to impact CTCF-binding (p<0.01, z-score: 6.01).
source: Comparing the height GWAS variants intersecting ATAC-seq peaks to 500 sets of random GWAS variants revealed an enrichment for variants that are predicted to impact CTCF-binding (p<0.01, z-score: 6.01, Figure 7c) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical enrichment of CTCF-disrupting variants.

claim: Height GWAS variants overlapping ATAC-seq peaks show strong enrichment for predicted PBX1 motifs (adjusted p value=1.91×10−108).
source: Additionally, we detected a strong enrichment of height GWAS variants overlapping predicted PBX1 motifs within ATAC-seq regions, when compared to height GWAS variants across the genome (adjusted p value=1.91×10−108, Supplementary file 9; see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical enrichment of PBX1 motifs at height GWAS variants.

claim: Height is highly heritable with typically 70-90% of variation in height within a population attributable to genetic variation.
source: Height has been studied for centuries as a model genetic trait, as it is easily measured and highly heritable (typically, 70–90% of variation in height within a population is attributable to genetic variation) (Silventoinen et al., 2003; Perola et al., 2007; Visscher et al., 2006; Visscher et al., 2007; Galton, 1886).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature on the heritability of height.

claim: GWAS for height have identified nearly 700 regions of the genome robustly associated with height.
source: GWAS for height are among the largest conducted thus far (sample sizes > 250,000) and have identified more associations than any other phenotype, with nearly 700 regions of the genome (or loci) robustly associated with height (Wood et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific GWAS study reporting the number of associated loci.

claim: Each height-associated variant has only a small effect on height (typically much less than 0.5 cm per allele).
source: Although each of the variants at these loci have only a small effect on height (typically much less than 0.5 cm per allele) (Wood et al., 2014), the genes within the associated loci as a group highlight important mechanisms influencing growth.
evidence: The manuscript cites the effect size of height variants from a GWAS study.

claim: Height variants are preferentially located near genes that are differentially expressed in the growth plate.
source: Height variants are also preferentially located near genes that are differentially expressed in the growth plate (Lui et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing enrichment of height variants near growth plate genes.

claim: Most GWAS variants (>80%) reside in non-coding regions.
source: Second, most GWAS variants (>80%) reside in non-coding regions (Gusev et al., 2014), with no nearby coding variants that can account for the associations.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on the genomic distribution of GWAS variants.

claim: GWAS variants tend to fall in regions that have particular epigenetically defined states such as enhancers or repressors.
source: It is also becoming increasingly clear that GWAS variants tend to fall in regions that have particular epigenetically defined states (such as enhancers or repressors) (Finucane et al., 2015; Farh et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing enrichment of GWAS variants in specific epigenetic states.

claim: The growth plate is located at the distal ends of long bones such as the femur.
source: The growth plate, located at the distal ends of long bones such as the femur, is among the most important tissues influencing height.
evidence: The manuscript describes the anatomical location of the growth plate.

claim: Chondrocytes in the growth plate reside in longitudinally oriented columns divided in zones (resting, proliferative, pre-hypertrophic, and hypertrophic).
source: Chondrocytes in the growth plate reside in longitudinally oriented columns divided in zones (resting, proliferative, pre-hypertrophic, and hypertrophic) each with important functions in allowing the bone to elongate and mature (see Liu et al., 2017 and Samsa et al., 2017 for reviews) (Liu et al., 2017; Samsa et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript describes the organization of the growth plate with citations to review articles.

claim: Growth plate chondrocyte differentiation and maturation promotes elongation of long bones, which ultimately determines much of human height.
source: This process of growth plate chondrocyte differentiation and maturation promotes elongation of long bones, which ultimately determines much of human height (Baron et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes the role of the growth plate in determining height with a citation.

claim: Disruption of Chsy1 in mice and humans leads to severe skeletal phenotypes including long bone length reductions.
source: Disruption of Chsy1 in mice and humans leads to severe skeletal phenotypes including long bone length reductions (Wilson et al., 2012; Temtamy et al., 1998; Tian et al., 2010; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing the phenotypic effects of CHSY1 disruption.

claim: Human mutations in CHSY1 result in Temtamy preaxial brachydactyly syndrome, characterized by short stature, preaxial brachydactyly, and hyperphalangism of digits 1–3.
source: Human mutations in CHSY1 result in Temtamy preaxial brachydactyly syndrome, characterized by short stature, preaxial brachydactyly, and hyperphalangism of digits 1–3 (45, 46), as well as a number of additional soft and hard tissue disorders.
evidence: The manuscript describes the clinical phenotype associated with CHSY1 mutations.

claim: HOXD13 is expressed in the growth plate.
source: Of the four variants, rs9920291 is predicted to alter HOXD13 binding, as suggested by data generated using universal protein binding microarray technology that demonstrates that the eight base-pair sequence matching the immediate rs9920291 locus disrupts in vitro binding by HOXD13 (Figure 6a, Supplementary file 7), a homeodomain transcription factor that is expressed in the growth plate (Kuss et al., 2014; Reno et al., 2016) and has known activating and repressive roles in skeletal development (Johnson and Tabin, 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing HOXD13 expression in the growth plate.

claim: HOXD13 has known activating and repressive roles in skeletal development.
source: Of the four variants, rs9920291 is predicted to alter HOXD13 binding, as suggested by data generated using universal protein binding microarray technology that demonstrates that the eight base-pair sequence matching the immediate rs9920291 locus disrupts in vitro binding by HOXD13 (Figure 6a, Supplementary file 7), a homeodomain transcription factor that is expressed in the growth plate (Kuss et al., 2014; Reno et al., 2016) and has known activating and repressive roles in skeletal development (Johnson and Tabin, 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing HOXD13's role in skeletal development.

claim: rs4911178 at the GDF5 locus resides in an ATAC-seq peak active in femoral growth plates.
source: We also highlight a previously identified height-associated variant (rs4911178) at the GDF5 locus, which resides in an ATAC-seq peak active in femoral growth plates (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript identifies a specific variant overlapping an ATAC-seq peak.

claim: The enhancer underlying rs4911178 drives GDF5 expression in growth plates and rs4911178 has allele-specific activity.
source: We have shown in separate work that the underlying enhancer drives GDF5 expression in growth plates and that rs4911178 has allele-specific activity(Capellini et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites their own separate work demonstrating functional validation of this variant.

claim: ATAC-seq requires approximately 50,000 cells.
source: To uncover mechanisms by which height GWAS variants function, we performed epigenetic profiling of murine femoral growth plates. The profiled open chromatin regions recapitulate known chondrocyte and skeletal biology, are enriched at height GWAS loci, particularly near differentially expressed growth plate genes, and enriched for binding motifs of transcription factors with roles in chondrocyte biology.
evidence: The abstract mentions that ATAC-seq allows profiling using relatively few cells.

claim: Integrating biologically relevant epigenetic information from growth plates with genetic association results can identify biological mechanisms important for human growth.
source: Thus, integrating biologically relevant epigenetic information (here, from growth plates) with genetic association results can identify biological mechanisms important for human growth.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this general statement about the approach.

claim: ATAC-seq datasets generated from mouse growth plate chondrocytes overlap previously identified signals of chondrocyte biology in the mouse and in humans.
source: Our analyses revealed that ATAC-seq datasets generated from mouse growth plate chondrocytes overlap previously identified signals of chondrocyte biology in the mouse, as well as in humans.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the validation of ATAC-seq data against known chondrocyte biology.

claim: ATAC-seq peaks acquired on femoral tissues show enrichment in human phenotypes related to the anatomy of femur.
source: While our datasets capture aspects of general chondrocyte biology, we also found that ATAC-seq peaks acquired on femoral tissues show enrichment in human phenotypes related to the anatomy of femur.
evidence: The discussion notes anatomical specificity of the enrichments.

claim: This finding points to a fine-grained, modularized control of skeletal element-specific biology.
source: This finding points to a fine-grained, modularized control of skeletal element-specific biology.
evidence: The discussion interprets the anatomical specificity as evidence for modular regulation.

claim: Over 80% of GWAS height loci are non-coding.
source: Given that over 80% of GWAS height loci are non-coding, our study demonstrates that height GWAS variants are significantly enriched in growth plate chondrocyte regulatory regions and that the majority reside in intergenic portions of the genome.
evidence: The discussion reiterates the non-coding nature of most height GWAS loci.

claim: Height GWAS variants are significantly enriched in growth plate chondrocyte regulatory regions.
source: Given that over 80% of GWAS height loci are non-coding, our study demonstrates that height GWAS variants are significantly enriched in growth plate chondrocyte regulatory regions and that the majority reside in intergenic portions of the genome.
evidence: The discussion summarizes the main finding of enrichment.

claim: The enrichment of height GWAS loci was not observed nearly as strongly in other chondrocyte or limb bud tissues.
source: Importantly, this enrichment of height GWAS loci was not observed nearly as strongly in other chondrocyte or limb bud tissues, which suggests that our dataset is capturing functional genetic variation influencing height that is not captured by other existing datasets.
evidence: The discussion emphasizes the specificity of the enrichment to their dataset.

claim: GWAS results for other traits/diseases that are not clearly related to growth/height did not show enrichment at the ATAC-seq peaks.
source: GWAS results for other traits/diseases that are not clearly related to growth/height did not show enrichment at the ATAC-seq peaks, demonstrating that the ATAC-seq peaks are specifically capturing growth/height biology.
evidence: The discussion notes the specificity of enrichment to height-related traits.

claim: Combining statistical fine-mapping and functional fine-mapping has allowed narrowing down to a much smaller subset of putatively causal variants for downstream functional testing.
source: Combining our statistical fine-mapping and functional fine-mapping has allowed us to narrow down to a much smaller subset of putatively causal variants for downstream functional testing.
evidence: The discussion describes the benefit of the integrated approach.

claim: Along with GDF5, CHSY1 is the only other height GWAS locus with functional validation.
source: To our knowledge, along with GDF5, this is the only other height GWAS locus with functional validation (Capellini et al., 2017).
evidence: The discussion claims novelty of the functional validation at CHSY1.

claim: ATAC-seq protocol was adapted from Buenrostro et al. (2013).
source: ATAC-seq protocol adapted from Buenrostro et al. (2013).
evidence: Figure 1 caption cites the source of the ATAC-seq protocol.

claim: Approximately 50,000 cells per sample were utilized for ATAC-seq.
source: Approximately 50,000 cells per sample were utilized for subsequent ATAC-seq.
evidence: Figure 1 caption specifies the number of cells used.

claim: Tissues were harvested just proximal or distal to the forming bone collar.
source: Tissues were harvested just proximal (red dotted lines in inset) or distal (blue dotted lines in inset) to the forming bone collar (outlined by dashed black lines).
evidence: Figure 1 caption describes the tissue dissection procedure.

claim: PICS was applied to perform statistical fine-mapping of the Wood et al. (2014) height GWAS results.
source: We applied PICS (Farh et al., 2015) to perform statistical fine-mapping of the (Wood et al., 2014) height GWAS results (Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical fine-mapping method used.
